summary:
North Sulawesi stands under the national framework applicable across Indonesia. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, separately criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with Aceh's punishments imposed under provincial religious law and applying to anyone present there, including foreign visitors. North Sulawesi does not carry that regime.

Physical risk at national level is documented. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party', arresting 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

North Sulawesi's own position is set against a documented pattern of provincial divergence. OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and discriminatory regional regulations examined eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It found much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set. North Sulawesi was not among the provinces examined.

Local reporting records both official-level engagement with the trans community and police conduct toward LGBT people in Manado. On Saturday 10 November 2012 a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach in Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS; Sinjal was quoted saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. No adverse official action is recorded in that account.

On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined Manado's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, Manado, between 08.00 and 10.00 WITA, with participation by SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation. The same reporting records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people, citing SALUT's account that a butch lesbian was groped during a raid, and that victims often do not report because they fear their families will not accept their orientation. The article reports no arrests or prosecutions.

Visibility carries stigma. A Konde.co interview published in February 2024 profiles Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara 2016-2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado, who states that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. No legal or police action appears anywhere in that account.
tangentialFactors:
Provincial divergence is a standing feature of Indonesia's regulatory landscape, and OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and regional regulations against LGBTIQ and women's rights identifies dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear as the recurring instruments. The variation runs across the eight focus provinces and the mapping states its findings are valid for regions beyond them, so a visitor to North Sulawesi should not assume that conditions reported from Aceh or Jakarta describe the province, nor that their absence is assured.

North Sulawesi's documented record contrasts with the raid pattern seen elsewhere in Indonesia. The 22 June 2025 villa operation near Bogor and the arrests at Puncak show that police action against private LGBT gatherings is a national practice, while the Manado reporting describes a different posture toward organised LGBT activity in public, alongside documented harassment during raids.

The province's trans community has been publicly visible for at least a decade: a waria pageant at Malalayang beach in 2012 was co-organised by a member of the national parliament and the provincial narcotics agency, and a province-level waria queen was elected in Manado in 2016. Public visibility is followed by media-driven stigma, as the Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara account sets out.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether North Sulawesi has enacted its own regional regulation (perda) restricting the conduct or public appearance of LGBT or waria residents is unresolved in this inventory. The OutRight Action International mapping examined eight focus provinces and North Sulawesi was not one of them, so no sourced statement about the province's local regulatory position can be made here.

No source in this inventory records prosecutions under the 2026 penal code, or any arrest or prosecution arising from the Manado raids or the LGBT action of 11 June 2016, within North Sulawesi. The absence of such reports in these sources is not evidence that none has occurred.

Whether police harassment of LGBT people described in Manado reporting continued after 2016 is unresolved; the sources stop at that period for raid-related conduct in the province.
